2. **Patrick's own name and age/birthplace assertions are unlinked.** a_008 (name "Patrick Flynn") and a_009 (age 15, born about 1845, Ireland) have no person_evidence entry. They are one-party facts about Patrick, so they belong on I1 at the same tier as pe_004. Until they are linked and materialized, the 1860 name and age are not on his tree person.

3. **The rest of the household was not extracted.** Only three assertions exist for this record. Mary (I3) and James (I4) are recorded children of Thomas with no 1860 appearance on file, and the record's other members are absent. I have not written anything. agent_returns.text:
I linked the 1850 census household of Thomas Flynn (record MXHY-TP4) to the three tree persons it names. The links are written as 16 `person_evidence` entries (pe_001 to pe_016), all sourced to src_001, and the household's facts are now on the tree people.

**Links**

| Persona in the census | Tree person | Confidence | Score | Assertions |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Patrick Flynn, child (P1) | I1 Patrick Flynn | probable | 0.24 | a_001, a_005, a_006, a_007, a_008, a_009 |
| Thomas Flynn, father (P2) | I2 Thomas Flynn | probable | 0.42 | a_010, a_011, a_012, a_013, and a_008 as the named father |
| Mary Flynn, mother (P3) | I3 Mary Flynn | confident | 0.89 | a_014, a_015, a_016, and a_009 and a_013 as the named mother |

- **Patrick:** The name, the ~1845 Ireland birth and the position as child of Thomas and Mary all fit the tree. The score is low because the tree attests only his birth, so I held the link at probable. No record other than this household bears on him yet.
- **Thomas:** The name and household position fit. The record gives no age or birthplace for him, so probable is the ceiling.
- **Mary:** Name, household position and the 0.89 score agree, so I set confident.
- **Residence:** The tree attests no residence for any of the three, so no move needed explaining.
- **Relationships:** The tree already holds the parent-child and couple edges for this family, so I wrote no new edges.

**Facts and warnings**

- Materialization added one fact per person and attached sources. It surfaced no conflicts.
- A warning on Thomas (I2) says his existing ~1818 Birth fact has no standard place. It is implausible, not impossible, and it predates this run.
- The birthplace check for Patrick did not run (`not_checked`), so the tree has not been checked for a birthplace conflict on him.

**Not linked**

Two other records in the project also name a Patrick Flynn or Thomas Flinn, and I left them alone. The first is the marriage record CFLT-9K2, whose Patrick is given a birthplace of Germany. The second is VRNT-7M3, a census record for Patrick Flinn. Both need their own identity review before they go to the tree.

---

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

Linked all ten assertions to the three members of the 1891 Leeds household, and materialized each person's facts onto the tree.

**Household check:** The tree has one other child of John and Ann, Thomas Carter (I3, baptised 1862). He is absent from this 1891 household. He may have left home, died, been enumerated elsewhere, or the household may be a different family. This needs an identity question, and I have not linked him.

**Links written (research.json, 12 entries, pe_008 to pe_019):**
- **John Carter (I1), confident, score 0.896.** Head of household. Birth about 1836 matches the tree, Leeds in 1861 and 1891, and his wife and son are the tree's own family edges. Covers a_001 to a_004, plus the head's name in the wife's and son's relationship assertions (a_007, a_010).
- **Albert Carter (I4), confident, score 0.815.** Son, age 7, matching the tree's birth about 1884 and his parents John and Ann. Covers a_008 to a_010.
- **Ann Carter (I2), probable, score 0.352.** Wife, Leeds in 1891, matching the tree's Couple edge with John. Covers a_005 to a_007. Probable only, because the score is low and she has only a residence fact in the tree.

**Flag for proof-conclusion:** The record gives Ann's age as 53 and Albert's as 7, a 46-year gap. The tree's warning for this is "implausible, not impossible", so I did not block the link. It is a question to settle in the conclusion, not a reason to reject her.

**Edges:** The tree already holds the couple and parent-child edges for John, Ann and Albert, so I wrote no new relationship edges.

**Warnings:** The person check on John, Ann and Albert returned one warning each about places not linked to a standard place. These are data-quality items, not identity problems. Ann's 45-year warning is the one above.

John and Albert are very likely the same people, and Ann is probably the same woman, though that match is weaker because the record gives her an age that is hard to square with being Albert's mother. Their son Thomas, who should be in the tree's family, is not in this household, so his whereabouts in 1891 is an open question. quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.
